Bone Physiology I — a living, self-rebuilding organ

Bone is not inert scaffolding — it is built, sensed, dissolved and rebuilt every day by four cells under hormonal control, and every disorder is that balance tipping. Decoded from Dr Ban's lecture, using its own figures.

§0Part A · orientation

Orientation — bone as a dynamic organ

Four cells, one balance — and everything else is that balance in action.

This lecture treats bone not as dead mineral but as a living tissue in constant turnover. It moves through four themes: the cells that make and break bone (§1), the structure those cells build and the properties it gives (§2), how bone is formed and grown (§3) and remodelled for life (§4), the hormones that control it all (§5), and the disorders that appear when the balance tips (§6).

Reasoning · why start with the cells

One idea runs through the entire lecture: bone is the sum of formation (osteoblasts) versus resorption (osteoclasts). Growth, remodelling, calcium balance and every disorder in §6 are just that balance shifted one way or the other. Learn the four cells first (§1) and the rest of the course is bookkeeping — who's winning, and why.

§1LO1 · cells

Bone cells

Four cells — one line that builds, one that demolishes, and two that stem and sense.

Four cell types, best understood as a construction crew working a two-part material — an organic scaffold and an inorganic mineral.

  • Osteoprogenitors — stem cells that differentiate into osteoblasts (the reserve supply of builders).
  • Osteoblasts — the builders: they secrete bone matrix (bone formation). The matrix has two parts — osteoid (organic, mainly collagen) and hydroxyapatite (inorganic, calcium + phosphate).
  • Osteocytes — former osteoblasts that became trapped in the matrix they laid down; they maintain and monitor bone (see §2).
  • Osteoclasts — the demolition cells: they secrete acid for bone resorption — proteases break down the osteoid proteins and HCl dissolves the hydroxyapatite mineral.

Plate 1.1 shows the four cells on a bone surface; Plate 1.2 shows osteoblasts and osteoclasts under the microscope.

Label Key
Osteoblasts
Line the surface; secrete osteoid + mineral (formation).
Osteoclasts
Large multinucleate cells resorbing bone (proteases + acid).
Fibrous periosteum / vessels
The covering and blood supply feeding the cells.
Label Key
Osteoblasts (▲)
Secreting bone matrix (*).
Osteoclasts (▲)
Secreting acid into a resorption bay (*).
Reasoning · two tools for a two-part material

Notice the symmetry. Bone matrix is organic (collagen) plus inorganic (mineral), so demolition needs two tools: the osteoclast uses proteases to cut the collagen and acid (HCl) to dissolve the mineral. Get either wrong and you get disease — fail to dissolve mineral (defective osteoclasts) and bone piles up thick but brittle (osteopetrosis, §6); dissolve too fast (osteoclast overactivity) and it thins (osteoporosis, §6). The cell defines the disorder.

Memory hook · read the suffix

-blast = build (osteoblasts lay matrix), -clast = carve (osteoclasts resorb), -cyte = caretaker (osteocytes maintain & sense). Osteoprogenitors are the reserve that becomes the builders.

§2LO1 · structure

Bone structure & properties

How the matrix is arranged — and why that arrangement makes bone strong.

§2.1Lamellae, compact & spongy bone

Bone matrix is laid down in lamellae — layers. Within them, osteocytes live in small spaces (lacunae) and extend fine processes through tiny canals (canaliculi); neighbouring osteocytes are wired together by gap junctions on those processes, so the buried cells can still talk to each other.

The arrangement of the lamellae defines the two bone types:

Compact vs spongy bone
Compact (cortical)Spongy (cancellous)
LamellaeConcentric → form osteonsIrregular → form trabeculae
Blood supplyFrom the central canal of each osteonFrom endosteal capillaries

Plate 2.1 shows lamellae, an osteon and trabeculae.

Label Key
Lamellae & osteon
Concentric layers around a central canal (compact bone).
Trabeculae
Irregular struts of spongy bone; osteocytes in lacunae/canaliculi throughout.

§2.2Why bone withstands force

This is the heart of LO1 — structure produces properties:

  • Compact bone. Its longitudinal collagen fibres are not parallel, so it resists torsional (twisting) force and has tensile (stretch) strength. Because collagen and hydroxyapatite are tightly bound, it also resists shear (slipping) force and has compressional strength.
  • Spongy bone. Its trabeculae are not randomly arranged — they align along the lines of stress and develop from microfractures caused by weight-bearing, resistance training and muscle pull, as part of continuous remodelling (§4).

Plate 2.2 shows the central-canal contents and the collagen orientation that resists twisting.

Label Key
Central canal
Artery/vein/nerve supplying the osteon.
Collagen fibres
Run in different directions (not parallel) → resist twisting.
Reasoning · structure → property (the LO1 link)

Every mechanical property traces to an arrangement. Cross-woven collagen (not parallel) is what defeats twisting — parallel fibres would unravel under torsion. Collagen glued to mineral is what defeats shear and compression — collagen alone bends, mineral alone shatters; bound together each covers the other's weakness. And trabeculae following stress lines means spongy bone puts material only where load demands it — maximum strength for minimum weight. Read a bone's arrangement and you can predict what force it's built to take.

Clinical / real-world · the osteocyte is the sensor

Those buried osteocytes wired by gap junctions are the tissue's strain gauges: they sense mechanical load and signal osteoblasts/osteoclasts to remodel accordingly (§4). It's why weight-bearing exercise thickens bone and why disuse, bed-rest or spaceflight thin it — the sensor stops reporting load, so bone is resorbed as "unneeded".

§3LO2 · formation

Bone formation & growth

From a cartilage template to a lengthening bone — development to adolescence.

Osteogenesis — the making of bone — runs from in utero to puberty. Long bones lengthen by replacing a cartilage model with bone.

Plate 3.1 shows osteogenesis from in utero to puberty.

Label Key
Cartilage model
A cartilage template is progressively replaced by bone (endochondral).
Primary/secondary centres
Ossification spreads from the shaft and the epiphyses.

§3.1Longitudinal growth

When? Continuously until the end of puberty. Where? At the epiphyseal (growth) plate, between the epiphyses (heads) and the diaphysis (shaft) of long bones. What? Chondrocytes lay down a cartilage foundation, then osteoblasts replace that cartilage with trabecular bone matrix — this is endochondral ossification. After puberty, the growth plate itself ossifies and lengthening stops.

Plate 3.2 shows the zones of the growth plate, from resting cartilage to new bone.

Label Key
Resting → proliferation → hypertrophic
Chondrocytes rest, divide, then enlarge.
Calcification → ossification
Cartilage calcifies & dies; osteoblasts lay new bone.
Reasoning · why build on a cartilage template

Why not lay bone directly? Because cartilage can grow from within (its cells divide and expand) whereas mineralised bone cannot. So the body grows a cartilage model that keeps lengthening at the plate, and osteoblasts follow behind, converting it to bone plank-by-plank. The growth plate is a moving frontier of cartilage-ahead, bone-behind — which is exactly why it's the weak point in children and the site that fails in rickets (§6).

§4LO3 · remodelling

Bone remodelling

A lifelong demolish-and-rebuild — coupled, sequenced, and load-driven.

Unlike growth, remodelling is lifelong: bone is continually resorbed by osteoclasts and rebuilt by osteoblasts, the two coupled so that demolition and construction stay in step.

Plate 4.1 shows the osteoblast–osteoclast interactions; Plate 4.2 the remodelling sequence (activation → resorption → reversal → formation).

Label Key
Osteoblast ↔ osteoclast
Coupled signalling (incl. RANKL/OPG) keeps resorption & formation in step.
Label Key
Activation → resorption
Osteoclasts recruited, dig a cavity.
Reversal → formation
Osteoblasts refill the cavity with new matrix.

§4.1Appositional growth

Growth in diameter (as opposed to length, §3) is appositional growth. When? Throughout life, correlated with tension and compression. Where? At the periosteum of the diaphysis, through the action of both osteoblasts AND osteoclasts — i.e. it is remodelling. What? Unlike longitudinal growth, appositional growth is a byproduct of development AND adaptation. Two theories explain its control:

  • Mechanostat — regulated by mechanical forces (muscle tension, weight-bearing, sporting use).
  • Sizostat — regulated by genetics, pre-determined and not dependent on mechanical forces.

Plate 4.3 shows apposition at the periosteum with resorption on the opposite surface.

Label Key
Periosteal apposition
Osteoblasts add bone on the outer surface.
Endosteal resorption
Osteoclasts remove bone within — widening the shaft.
Reasoning · why remodelling never stops

Remodelling does three jobs at once: it repairs microdamage before it becomes a fracture, it reshapes bone to current load (the mechanostat idea — trabeculae realign, the shaft thickens where muscles pull), and it releases or stores calcium on demand (§5). That's why it must run for life, and why it's the process hijacked in Paget's disease (§6, dysfunctional osteoclasts) and tuned by every hormone in §5.

Clinical / real-world · use it or lose it

The mechanostat is clinical reality: load builds bone, disuse loses it. Athletes' loaded bones are denser; immobilised limbs, prolonged bed-rest and microgravity all drive rapid bone loss — the same logic behind prescribing weight-bearing exercise to protect against osteoporosis (§6).

§5LO3 · hormones

Bone homeostasis — hormonal control

Bone is the body's calcium bank; hormones decide when to deposit and when to withdraw.

The skeleton holds ~99% of the body's calcium, so controlling blood calcium means controlling bone. Three hormones set the balance.

§5.1Calcium homeostasis — the three hormones

The calcium-regulating hormones
HormoneSourceBlood CaBone effect
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)Parathyroid glands↑Bone resorption
Calcitriol (vitamin D3)Kidneys (stimulated by PTH)↑Bone resorption
CalcitoninThyroid gland↓Bone formation

Plate 5.1 traces calcium between gut, blood, kidney and bone under these hormones.

Label Key
Bone (99% of Ca)
The reservoir; PTH/calcitriol withdraw Ca (resorb), calcitonin deposits.
Gut & kidney
Absorption & renal handling tune blood [Ca] (~2.5 mM).

§5.2PTH — the dual-personality hormone

PTH is not simply "bad for bone". Its effect flips with the pattern of exposure:

  • Continuous exposure → catabolic (net resorption): PTH raises RANKL and lowers OPG, driving osteoclasts → blood Ca increases.
  • Intermittent exposure → anabolic (net formation): a daily low dose instead ↑ osteoblast differentiation and ↓ osteoblast apoptosis → this is the basis of teriparatide, an osteoporosis therapy.

Plate 5.2 contrasts the catabolic and anabolic effects of PTH.

Label Key
Continuous → catabolic
↑RANKL, ↓OPG → resorption, ↑blood Ca.
Intermittent → anabolic
↑OB differentiation, ↓OB apoptosis → formation (teriparatide).
Reasoning · RANKL/OPG is the master switch

Almost every hormone here acts through one lever: the RANKL:OPG ratio. RANKL activates osteoclasts; OPG is a decoy that blocks it. So ↑RANKL / ↓OPG = resorption (PTH continuous, glucocorticoids) and ↓RANKL / ↑OPG = formation (estrogens, androgens). Learn that one switch and the whole hormone table (§5.4) reads itself. It also explains PTH's paradox: a constant signal keeps the switch on (resorption), but a pulse is read by osteoblasts instead — same hormone, opposite result.

§5.3Vitamin D3 (calcitriol)

Vitamin D3 must be activated in three steps before it can regulate calcium:

  1. Cholecalciferol — from the diet or made in the skin (UV-induced).
  2. 25-hydroxycholecalciferol — converted in the liver.
  3. 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol) — the active hormone, made in the kidney (PTH-induced).

Plate 5.3 shows the skin → liver → kidney activation pathway.

Label Key
Skin/diet → liver
Cholecalciferol → 25-hydroxycholecalciferol.
Kidney (PTH-induced)
→ 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (active calcitriol).
Clinical / real-world · where vitamin D fails

Because activation is a three-organ relay, a calcium deficiency can originate in the skin, liver OR kidney — each step is a possible fault. And since step 1 needs UV, people living above 37°N or below 37°S latitude may not get enough sun year-round and are advised to supplement — a direct cause of osteomalacia/rickets (§6).

§5.4The full hormone table

Hormones involved in remodelling
HormoneRegulationNet effect
Growth hormone (GH)↑ osteoblast proliferation; ↑ apposition; ↑ longitudinal growthFormation
Thyroid hormone (TH)↑ OB differentiation; ↓ OB proliferation; ↑ osteoclast activityResorption
Calcitonin↓ osteoclast activityFormation
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)↑ RANKL, ↓ OPGResorption
Glucocorticoids (e.g. cortisol)↑ RANKL, ↓ OPGResorption
Estrogens↓ RANKL, ↑ OPG; ↑ osteoclast apoptosisFormation
Androgens (e.g. testosterone)↓ RANKL, ↑ OPG; ↑ apposition; ↑ longitudinal growthFormation
Clinical / real-world · reading the table as disease

Each row predicts a disorder (§6). Estrogens favour formation → losing them at menopause unleashes resorption → post-menopausal osteoporosis. Glucocorticoids favour resorption → excess cortisol (Cushing's, or steroid therapy) → osteoporosis. Excess GH → gigantism (pre-puberty) or acromegaly (post-puberty). The hormone table is the disorder list in advance.

§6LO4 · disorders

Disorders of bone

Every disorder is a cell, hormone or matrix component from §1–§5 gone wrong.

§6.1Bone mineral density & how we measure it

Peak bone mass is achieved by 25–30 years and stays stable to about 40; it is 60–80% genetic, with the rest environmental (diet, exercise). Density is measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA), scored by age:

  • Z-score — compares you to a reference of the same age and sex (used for M <50 years, F <menopause).
  • T-score — compares you to a peak-bone-mass reference of the same sex (used for M >50 years, F >menopause).
  • A score of −2.5 or less indicates osteoporosis.

Plate 6.1 shows bone mass rising to a peak then declining (faster after menopause) toward osteopenia/osteoporosis.

Label Key
Peak bone mass
Reached ~25–30; higher peak = more reserve.
Decline / menopause
Loss accelerates (esp. after menopause) → osteopenia → osteoporosis.

Label Key

Label Key

Reasoning · trace each back to §1–§5

None of these is new — each is a §1–§5 mechanism failing. Osteoporosis = osteoclasts unchecked because endocrine suppression fell (lost estrogen at menopause, §5.4). Osteomalacia = the vitamin-D relay (§5.3) breaks, so matrix is laid but not mineralised — soft bone. Rickets = the same deficiency in a child, so it also wrecks the growth plate (§3) → bowed legs. Brown tumour = too much PTH (§5.2) resorbing bone. Gigantism/acromegaly = too much GH (§5.4) driving growth/apposition. Name the broken step and you've named the disease.

Plate 6.5 osteogenesis imperfecta; Plate 6.6 Paget's disease; Plate 6.7 osteopetrosis.

Label Key
Fragile bones

Label Key

Clinical / real-world · the osteoclast paradox — thick can mean weak

Osteopetrosis is the counter-intuitive one that proves §1's logic. Defective osteoclasts can't resorb, so bone accumulates — thick and dense on X-ray, yet brittle and weak (it's never remodelled, so microdamage is never repaired, §4). Worse, unresorbed bone fills the medullary cavity, crowding out marrow → anaemia. More bone is not stronger bone — balance is. Compare osteogenesis imperfecta, where the collagen scaffold (§1) is faulty, so bones are low-mass and shatter (the classic "brittle bone disease").

R Recall checklist — Bone Physiology I
  • Cells — osteoprogenitor → osteoblast (osteoid=collagen + hydroxyapatite=Ca+phosphate) → osteocyte (in matrix); osteoclast resorbs (proteases + HCl).
  • Structure — lamellae; osteocytes in lacunae, canaliculi, gap junctions. Compact = osteons + central canal; spongy = trabeculae + endosteal capillaries.
  • Properties — compact: non-parallel collagen (torsion/tensile), collagen+mineral bound (shear/compression). Spongy: trabeculae align to stress lines from microfractures.
  • Formation — osteogenesis in utero→puberty; longitudinal growth at the epiphyseal plate (endochondral: chondrocytes → osteoblasts); plate ossifies after puberty.
  • Remodelling — lifelong, coupled resorption→formation; appositional growth at periosteum (osteoblasts+osteoclasts); mechanostat vs sizostat.
  • Hormones — Ca↑: PTH, calcitriol (resorption); Ca↓: calcitonin (formation). PTH continuous=catabolic / intermittent=anabolic (teriparatide). Vit D: skin→liver→kidney. RANKL↑/OPG↓ = resorption; RANKL↓/OPG↑ = formation.
  • Disorders — DEXA, T-score ≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis. Metabolic: osteoporosis, osteomalacia, rickets, brown tumour, gigantism/acromegaly, Cushing's. Genetic: OI (collagen I), Paget's (dysfunctional OC), osteopetrosis (defective OC → dense-but-weak + anaemia), Marfan (fibrillin I).
